subject: literature
title: Existentialism (c. 1943–1960): literature after the occupation
dek: After high modernism’s broken sentence came war, occupation, and Liberation. In Paris a press word — existentialism — stuck to novels and plays of situation, to Les Temps modernes, and to a public break between Camus and Sartre.

thumb.alt: American infantry of the 28th Division march down the Champs-Élysées toward the Arc de Triomphe, 29 August 1944.

hero.alt: Rows of American soldiers in helmets march down a tree-lined Paris avenue; the Arc de Triomphe stands in the distance.
hero.caption: American troops of the 28th Infantry Division on the Champs-Élysées, 29 August 1944, with the Arc de Triomphe ahead. Paris had been liberated a few days earlier. This lesson’s literature is postwar in a city that had just been occupied. The photograph is a parade, not a café.
hero.credit: Poinsett / U.S. Army Signal Corps / public domain

honesty: “Existentialism” is a later press and classroom label. Sartre and Beauvoir used it; Camus did not accept it as a school name for himself. Gabriel Marcel had already used related language in 1943. This lesson looks out from occupied and post-Liberation Paris — cafés, a magazine, novels and plays of situation — then notices other 1950s literatures that were running at the same time. They are contemporaneous events, not a West-plus-Asia formula. High modernism is the previous Thursday in this archive; it is not repeated here.

timeline.label: La Nausée
timeline.detail: Sartre’s novel appears. A forerunner written before the war that later readers folded into the postwar label.

timeline.label: L’Étranger / L’Être et le Néant
timeline.detail: Camus’s novel (1942). Sartre’s Being and Nothingness (1943). Occupation Paris is the room, not only the theory.

timeline.label: Huis clos / Liberation
timeline.detail: No Exit premieres at the Théâtre du Vieux-Colombier, 27 May. Paris is liberated in August.

timeline.label: Les Temps modernes
timeline.detail: First issue, October. Named after Chaplin’s Modern Times. A magazine becomes an institution.

timeline.label: La Peste / Le Deuxième Sexe
timeline.detail: Camus’s The Plague (1947). Beauvoir’s The Second Sex (1949), first serialized in Les Temps modernes.

timeline.label: The break
timeline.detail: Camus’s The Rebel (1951). Francis Jeanson’s review in Les Temps modernes (May 1952); Camus and Sartre exchange open letters (August). Friendship ends in public.

timeline.label: Elsewhere / Paris
timeline.detail: Ellison’s Invisible Man (1952). Fanon’s Black Skin, White Masks (1952). Wright’s The Outsider (1953), written in Paris.

timeline.label: The label thins
timeline.detail: Structuralism and other Paris fashions take the prestige slot. The press word goes stale. This lesson stops before a full postmodernism chapter.

fun_fact.title: Les Temps modernes took its name from a Chaplin film
fun_fact.text: When Sartre’s circle settled on a title for their new review in late 1944, they chose Les Temps modernes — Modern Times — after Charlie Chaplin’s 1936 film. The first issue appeared in October 1945, after paper shortages delayed it. The board included Sartre, Beauvoir, Maurice Merleau-Ponty, Raymond Aron, Michel Leiris, Albert Ollivier, and Jean Paulhan. A comedy about factory life became the letterhead of a magazine that argued for littérature engagée. The film is still the easier object to name than the paper ration.

glossary.explain: Press and classroom name for a mid-twentieth-century cluster of novels, plays, and philosophy that treated freedom, situation, and bad faith as public problems. Sartre and Beauvoir used the word; Camus did not accept it as a school label for himself.

Earlier twentieth-century formal experiment — Woolf, Joyce, Eliot, and others — treated in this archive’s Thursday lesson of that name. The immediate literary past before the 1930s political novel and the war.
Sartre’s theatre and novel term: a concrete set of constraints and choices, not an abstract theme. A play of situation puts characters into a closed room of consequences.
Sartre’s name for drama built around a concrete dilemma rather than psychological portrait alone. Huis clos is the usual exhibit.
French for commitment: the claim that writing is not neutral. Sartre’s Qu’est-ce que la littérature? and Les Temps modernes made engagement a magazine program.
Sartre’s bad faith: lying to oneself about freedom or facticity — pretending one has no choice, or pretending one has no past. The café waiter who overplays being a waiter is the classroom example.
Camus’s word for the clash between the human demand for meaning and a world that does not answer it. Not a synonym for nihilism in his essays.
German occupation of France, 1940–44. The political weather for Huis clos, Combat, and the cafés that still had heat.
The freeing of Paris in August 1944 and the wider end of occupation. The public after against which Les Temps modernes launched.
Literary-political review founded by Sartre’s circle; first issue October 1945; titled after Chaplin’s Modern Times. Serialized parts of The Second Sex; published the 1952 Camus–Sartre break.
Café on Boulevard Saint-Germain. During the Occupation, Sartre and Beauvoir worked there because the upstairs rooms stayed heated when many hotels did not.
Café opposite the Flore on the Place Saint-Germain-des-Prés side of the boulevard. The other famous terrace; later a tourist address.
Left-Bank neighborhood around the old abbey church. The cafés, hotels, and Gallimard offices that made the press story of existentialism a place name.
Theatre at 21 rue du Vieux-Colombier. Huis clos premiered there on 27 May 1944.
Philosopher and writer (1905–1980). La Nausée (1938), Being and Nothingness (1943), Huis clos (1944), Les Temps modernes. Public face of the label he partly accepted.
Writer and philosopher (1908–1986). The Second Sex (1949); novels and memoirs; co-founder of Les Temps modernes. Not only “Sartre’s partner.”
Writer (1913–1960). L’Étranger (1942), The Myth of Sisyphus (1942), The Plague (1947), The Rebel (1951). Editor at Combat; broke with Sartre in 1952. Refused the school label “existentialist.”
Philosopher (1908–1961). Phenomenology of Perception (1945); early Temps modernes editor. Adjacent to the literary circle, not a novelist of situation.
Writer and playwright (1910–1986). Thief, prisoner, then Gallimard author. Sartre’s long Saint Genet (1952) made him a philosophical exhibit as well as a literary one.
Writer (1906–1989). Waiting for Godot (1953 Paris premiere). Adjacent absurdist theatre, not the Sartre school; named because the same years put both on Paris stages.
Psychiatrist and writer (1925–1961). Black Skin, White Masks (1952); The Wretched of the Earth (1961) at the edge of this lesson’s dates.
American novelist (1908–1960). Native Son (1940); settled in Paris after the war; The Outsider (1953). Named in the 1930s political past and in the Paris years.
American novelist (1914–1994). Invisible Man (1952). Jim Crow and Harlem, not Saint-Germain.
Critic and Temps modernes editor. His May 1952 review of The Rebel triggered Camus’s letter to “Monsieur le Directeur.”
Philosopher and journalist (1905–1983). On the first Temps modernes board; later broke with Sartre’s politics. Named as board fact, not as a deep dive.
Editor (1884–1968). Gallimard / NRF figure on the first Temps modernes board.
Writer and ethnographer (1901–1990). On the first Temps modernes board.
Filmmaker. Modern Times (1936) gave Les Temps modernes its title.
Chaplin film, 1936. The magazine’s namesake.
Paris publisher. Issued many of the books in this lesson and housed early Temps modernes offices.
Resistance and postwar newspaper. Camus was a leading editorial voice there during and after the Liberation.
Sartre novel, 1938. Prewar forerunner; Roquentin’s nausea at contingency. Place it before 1943, not as a Liberation product.
Sartre’s Being and Nothingness, 1943. Philosophical treatise written under occupation; bad faith and freedom as technical terms.
Camus novel, 1942 (English: The Stranger / The Outsider). Meursault in Algiers; flat prose; a killing on a beach; a trial that moralizes sunlight and manners.
Sartre play, premiered 27 May 1944 at the Vieux-Colombier. Three people locked in a room; “Hell is other people.”
Camus essay, 1942 (The Myth of Sisyphus). The absurd as a starting problem, not a slogan on a beret.
Camus novel, 1947 (The Plague). Oran under epidemic; read then and later as occupation allegory and as plague narrative.
Beauvoir’s The Second Sex, 1949. Two volumes: history and myth, then lived experience. Method from philosophy and reportage, not only a feminist label.
Camus’s The Rebel, 1951. Essay on revolt and limits; attacked Stalinist apologetics; the book Jeanson reviewed.
Fanon’s Black Skin, White Masks, 1952. Colonial racism as lived psychic situation.
Fanon’s The Wretched of the Earth, 1961. At the far edge of this lesson’s dates; named only as later edge.
Richard Wright novel, 1953, written in Paris. American existential thriller; not Camus’s L’Étranger under another title.
Ralph Ellison novel, 1952. Narrator’s invisibility under American racism. Same year as Fanon’s first book; different city.
Wright novel, 1940. Named as 1930s–40s political-novel past, not as the Paris chapter.
Orwell’s 1938 account of the Spanish Civil War. Named as 1930s political writing in the Before section.
Steinbeck novel, 1939. Named briefly as 1930s political fiction.
British writer (1903–1950). Named for the 1930s political novel/reportage past.
American novelist (1902–1968). Named for The Grapes of Wrath as 1930s political fiction.
British press label for mid-1950s writers and playwrights — Osborne’s Look Back in Anger (1956) as the usual stage marker. Class anger in London, not Paris cafés.
Playwright (1929–1994). Look Back in Anger, Royal Court Theatre, 1956.
Osborne play, 1956. The Angry Young Men stage date.
London theatre in Sloane Square. Look Back in Anger premiered there.

Japanese writer (1924–1993). The Woman in the Dunes (1962) is just after this lesson’s center; named as a contemporaneous writer working related problems of confinement and absurdity, not as a Sartre disciple.
Japanese novelist (1935–2023). Early work from the late 1950s; read Sartre as a French literature student. Contemporaneous, not a twin.
Abe novel, 1962. Sand pit as situation. Named at the edge of the dates.
1960s Paris intellectual fashion — Lévi-Strauss and others — that took prestige as the existentialist label went stale. Named only as After, not as a full lesson.
Sartre’s What Is Literature?, 1948 (parts earlier in Temps modernes). Engagement as a theory of prose.
Sartre’s long 1952 study of Jean Genet. A philosophical biography that made Genet a case.
Beckett play; Paris premiere 1953. Absurd theatre adjacent to this lesson.
Legal and customary racial segregation in the United States. The American situation behind Invisible Man.
City where L’Étranger is set. French Algeria, not Paris.
Algerian city setting of The Plague.
French philosopher (1889–1973). Used “existentialism” as a label in 1943; later distanced himself from Sartre’s atheist version.
Sartre’s public lecture of 29 October 1945, later a short book. The event that made the press word hard to unsay.

sections.title: A broken sentence, then a political decade, then a war

blocks.text: High modernism had already broken the ordinary novel sentence. Woolf, Joyce, and Eliot made time and attention into structure; vernacular Chinese modernism was running in the same years. That work is another Thursday in this archive. What stands between those experiments and the books in this lesson is not a clean handover. The 1930s put politics back into the foreground of fiction and reportage: George Orwell’s Homage to Catalonia (1938), Richard Wright’s Native Son (1940), John Steinbeck’s The Grapes of Wrath (1939). Those titles are named here as the immediate literary past, not as a second lesson. Then came defeat, occupation, collaboration, deportation, and camps. By 1944 the question for many French writers was not how to fragment a day on the page. It was what a person was free to do inside a situation that had already chosen them.

blocks.alt: The Romanesque tower and dark spire of the church of Saint-Germain-des-Prés above lower stone buildings and a green Paris news kiosk, photographed in 2022.
blocks.caption: The abbey church of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, photographed in November 2022. The cafés that sold the postwar story sit on the boulevard beside this tower. The cars and the news kiosk are later. The address is the fact.
blocks.credit: Diego Delso / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 4.0

blocks.text: Sartre’s novel La Nausée had already appeared in 1938. It belongs in this lesson as a forerunner, not as a Liberation product. The occupation years then forced the argument into public rooms: heated cafés when hotels were cold, a theatre still open in May 1944, a Resistance paper, and, after August, a city that had to invent what “after” meant.

sections.title: Occupied Paris, Liberation, and a press word

blocks.text: The trigger is concrete. Under occupation, Sartre and Beauvoir wrote at the Café de Flore because the upper floor stayed warm when charcoal and hotel heating failed. Huis clos — No Exit — opened at the Théâtre du Vieux-Colombier on 27 May 1944, still under German control of the city. Three characters locked in a Second Empire drawing room discover that they are one another’s torture. The line everyone remembers, “Hell is other people,” is a situation joke with philosophical teeth, not a poster about hating company. In August the city was liberated. The photographs of soldiers on the Champs-Élysées are the public fact. The literary fact is what a circle of writers did with the next fifteen years.

blocks.alt: Looking through a café window at red banquettes, arched mirrors, waiters in long white aprons, and a pastry case under warm lamps.
blocks.caption: Café de Flore, photographed through the window on 4 June 2015. Red banquettes, waiters in long aprons, a pastry case, a no-smoking sticker on the glass. This is the later tourist interior. During the Occupation the same address was a heated workplace for Sartre and Beauvoir. The caption has to say both things.

blocks.alt: Sidewalk terrace of Les Deux Magots under a green awning with gold lettering, round tables and woven chairs, a waiter near the door.
blocks.caption: Les Deux Magots, Boulevard Saint-Germain, 6 September 2011. The green awning and the name in gold are the postcard. Sartre’s circle also used this terrace; after the war the two cafés became interchangeable in the press. The timestamp in the corner is the photographer’s; the building is older.
blocks.credit: Britchi Mirela / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 3.0

blocks.text: In October 1945 Les Temps modernes published its first issue. The title came from Chaplin’s Modern Times. Sartre directed; the board included Beauvoir, Merleau-Ponty, Aron, Leiris, Ollivier, and Paulhan. Camus was busy with Combat and was not on that masthead. The magazine serialized fiction and argument, printed Sartre’s claims for littérature engagée, and later carried chapters of Beauvoir’s The Second Sex. It was an institution in the plain sense: an office, a paper ration, a telephone number printed for visitors, and a place where a review could end a friendship in public.

blocks.alt: Street entrance of the Théâtre du Vieux-Colombier with gold lettering, a dark modern canopy, red light inside the glass doors, a parked scooter and pedestrians.
blocks.caption: Théâtre du Vieux-Colombier, 21 rue du Vieux-Colombier, September 2018. The gold letters and the dove emblems mark the house where Huis clos premiered on 27 May 1944. The scooter, the Lucrèce Borgia poster, and the red lobby light are later. The address is the 1944 fact.

blocks.text: The word “existentialism” itself was partly a journalist’s convenience. Gabriel Marcel had used related language in 1943. On 29 October 1945 Sartre gave the lecture later published as Existentialism Is a Humanism; the room was crowded enough that the newspapers treated the word as a brand. Sartre and Beauvoir accepted a version of the name in public; Camus kept saying he was not an existentialist in Sartre’s sense. The useful literary unit is not the beret. It is the novel and the play of situation: a character thrown into a set of constraints — a beach, a plague city, a locked room, a sexed body, a colonized gaze — and forced to choose without a guaranteed script.

sections.title: Novels and plays of situation — and three to read slowly

blocks.text: Name the shelf without pretending it is one committee. Sartre: La Nausée (1938 forerunner), Being and Nothingness (1943), Huis clos (1944), the Temps modernes editorials, What Is Literature? (1948), Saint Genet (1952). Beauvoir: novels, memoirs, and The Second Sex (1949). Camus: L’Étranger (1942), The Myth of Sisyphus (1942), The Plague (1947), The Rebel (1951). Beside them: Genet’s plays and prose; Beckett’s Waiting for Godot (Paris, 1953), adjacent absurd theatre rather than Sartre’s school; Merleau-Ponty’s philosophy in the same offices; Fanon’s Black Skin, White Masks (1952), with The Wretched of the Earth (1961) at the far edge; Richard Wright in Paris writing The Outsider (1953). In Japan, Ōe Kenzaburō was reading French literature and Sartre as a student in the late 1950s; Abe Kōbō’s The Woman in the Dunes (1962) sits just after this lesson’s center and works a confinement problem that later readers filed beside the absurd. Those Japanese names are contemporaneous writers facing related pressures after defeat and occupation — not an assigned Asian twin for a Paris trio.

people.name: Jean-Paul Sartre
people.alt: Jean-Paul Sartre in Venice, August 1967, glasses, open shirt, standing before a window with red geraniums.
people.caption: Venice, August 1967 — later than the Occupation café years. The face the cameras kept.
people.text: Novelist, playwright, philosopher, magazine director. He made “situation” and “bad faith” into tools a general reader could argue with. The 1967 photograph is not a 1944 document; it is a free portrait of the public man the earlier decade produced.

people.name: Simone de Beauvoir
people.text: Philosopher and novelist; co-founder of Les Temps modernes. The Second Sex (1949) is a book of method — history, myth, lived reports — as much as it is a founding feminist text later waves would claim. A clearly free studio portrait from the 1940s is hard to license cleanly; this lesson does not invent one.

people.name: Albert Camus
people.text: Novelist, playwright, Combat editor. The Stranger and The Plague made the absurd and revolt readable as stories. He rejected the school name “existentialist,” then broke with Sartre in 1952 over The Rebel. Studio Harcourt’s 1945 portrait is treated as public domain in France on collective-work grounds; this capsule skips it rather than lean on a thin cross-border claim.

people.name: Richard Wright
people.alt: Studio portrait of Richard Wright in a light tweed jacket and dark tie, photographed by Carl Van Vechten in 1939.
people.caption: Carl Van Vechten’s studio portrait, 23 June 1939 — before Wright’s Paris years. The face that Native Son made public.
people.credit: Carl Van Vechten / Library of Congress / public domain
people.text: Native Son (1940) belongs to the political-novel past. After the war he lived in Paris, knew Sartre and Beauvoir, and published The Outsider (1953). An American writer in the same cafés, not a French mascot.

blocks.text: Deepen three objects. First, The Stranger. Camus’s French is short, declarative, and cool: “Mother died today. Or maybe yesterday, I don’t know.” Meursault narrates heat, swimming, sex, and a funeral as if they were weather reports. The killing on the Algiers beach arrives with the same flatness. The trial then invents a moral personality the prose has refused to supply — he did not cry at his mother’s funeral, therefore he is a monster. The book’s force is technical: a style that will not perform the remorse the court demands. That is how the absurd gets into the sentences, not only into an essay.

Second, The Second Sex. Beauvoir’s 1949 book is two volumes: how “woman” was made in biology talk, history, and myth, then how girls and women live that making. The famous line — one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman — is a claim about situation and becoming, written by a philosopher who had already co-run a magazine. Later Second Wave feminism would take the book as an ancestor; that reception is real. The book itself is also literature and method: long readings, case descriptions, a refusal to treat “woman” as a timeless essence. Put it beside Huis clos and L’Étranger as a postwar Paris object, not only as a chapter in a feminism syllabus.

Third, the Camus–Sartre break. The Rebel appeared in 1951. In May 1952 Francis Jeanson reviewed it harshly in Les Temps modernes. Camus answered with a letter addressed not to Jeanson but to “Monsieur le Directeur” — Sartre. In the August issue Sartre answered at length and with personal heat. The friendship ended in the magazine that had defined their public. The argument was about revolt, history, and Marxism; it was also about who owned the postwar moral microphone. Treat it as a literary-political fact with dates, not as a celebrity feud with no content.

While Paris argued about engagement, other literatures were not waiting for a French cue card. In the United States, Ralph Ellison’s Invisible Man (1952) sent a nameless narrator through a Southern college, a Harlem movement, and a basement with 1,369 lights. The book’s problem is American racial invisibility under Jim Crow and Northern hypocrisy. It is not a translation of Being and Nothingness. Gordon Parks’s wartime Harlem photographs — a newsboy before posters for Adam Clayton Powell Jr. and the Pittsburgh Courier — are the visual weather of that American situation, taken a decade earlier and still the right street.

blocks.alt: A young Black newsboy in a wool coat and knit cap stands before a newsstand covered with posters, including one for Adam Powell and People’s Voice; OWI serial number at the top.
blocks.caption: Harlem newsboy, May 1943, photographed by Gordon Parks for the U.S. Office of War Information. Posters for Adam Clayton Powell Jr.’s People’s Voice tour and a Pittsburgh Courier clipping sit behind him; the OWI serial number is printed at the top of the negative. This is New York under wartime Jim Crow, the American “elsewhere” for Invisible Man — not a Paris café.
blocks.credit: Gordon Parks / U.S. Office of War Information / Library of Congress / public domain

blocks.text: In Britain, the press found “Angry Young Men” after John Osborne’s Look Back in Anger opened at the Royal Court Theatre in 1956. Class resentment and a kitchen sink are the furniture; Saint-Germain is not. In Japan, writers who had lived defeat and occupation were publishing through the 1950s; Ōe’s early fiction and Abe’s later sand-pit novel are named here as parallel pressures, not as proof that existentialism was universal. Latin American boom novels of the 1960s are later and are not forced into this capsule.

sections.title: The label thins; the books remain

blocks.text: By about 1960 the Paris prestige slot was moving. Structuralism — Lévi-Strauss and the arguments that followed — took the seminar glamour. “Existentialist” became a costume in the newspapers: a jazz cellar, a black sweater, a simplified Sartre. Camus died in a car crash on 4 January 1960. Sartre lived long enough to refuse the Nobel Prize in 1964 and to become a different kind of public monument. The useful after is not yet postmodernism as a full lesson. It is this: the novels and plays still work when the beret joke is gone, and other cities had never needed the beret to write their own situations.
If this archive takes another Thursday further on, it will not be to complete a French syllabus. It will be because another year also happened.
When a magazine can end a friendship in public, what is literature being asked to do that a private letter cannot?
